title: Empirical Integration of a Formal Network Verifier as an Oracle inside an LLM Generate–Verify–Repair Loop: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired within-task experiment to test whether embedding a formal-network verifier as an oracle inside a Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) loop improves detection/rejection of unsafe or incorrect LLM-generated network configurations and increases automated repair success versus single-shot generation. We ran N=270 intent→configuration tasks (3 vendor-style syntaxes × 3 topology templates × 30 tasks) with a paired baseline (single-shot generation) and guarded (GVR: generate → verifier → bounded LLM repair if rejected) condition using gpt-5-mini. A deterministic netops validator/emulator provided ground truth. All planned executions completed (540 episodes). Observed baseline and guarded verifier-accepted rates were both 270/270 (100%), giving a paired difference of 0.00 (95% CI 0.00–0.00, exact McNemar two-sided p=1.0). The preregistered primary estimand therefore shows no improvement from the inserted verifier under these tasks and model settings. We report the full preregistration, execution manifest, analysis artifacts, and provenance; interpret this null result in terms of dataset difficulty, model-generator strength, and verifier design; and identify limitations and next steps for stronger operational validation.

sections.introduction: Motivation: LLMs promise intent-driven NetOps automation but their stochastic generations risk unsafe or incorrect configuration actions. Prior generate–verify–repair (GVR) proposals interpose deterministic oracles between stochastic generators and execution to reduce risk. Research question (preregistered): Does embedding a formal-network verifier as an oracle inside a bounded GVR loop increase detection/rejection of unsafe or incorrect LLM-generated network configurations and improve bounded repair success versus single-shot generation? Contributions: (1) a preregistered paired empirical study (study_id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1); (2) a public synthetic intent→configuration task suite and Dockerized emulator/validator pipeline used for deterministic ground truth; (3) complete execution and analysis artifacts showing the observed outcome and provenance; (4) an evidence-grounded discussion of why the observed null effect arose and operational implications.
sections.related_work: This study is positioned at the intersection of LLM-assisted configuration generation and verified generate–verify–repair architectures. We preregistered the design guided by prior GVR and verifier-forcing work (see Convergent Correctness [doi:10.2139/ssrn.6754899] and Weighted NetKAT for quantitative verification primitives [doi:10.1145/3808318]). We also relied on extant NetOps intent/configuration and verification literature for task design and validator semantics (preregistration evidence list). Unlike benchmarking-only papers, our focus is the operational reliability effect of inserting a deterministic verifier as an oracle inside an automated repair loop under a fixed budget.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and experimental plan: preregistered (study_id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1; preregistration SHA-256 8ae7fbadf89e5d56671560e43f03c4a92ad5f8c9b8586ac8eb3cc3c8fa00a1c0). Design: paired within-task (N=270 tasks), each task executed in both conditions: baseline (single-shot generation) and guarded (generate → deterministic netops verifier oracle → if rejected, a single bounded LLM repair call). Model and prompting: gpt-5-mini (provider: openai_responses), deterministic prompt templates and fixed seeds recorded. Validator/emulator: Dockerized Kathará/Mininet-based emulator and a deterministic netops validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) providing strict intent-constraint checks; a 20% validation subset (54 tasks) was reserved for verifier vs emulator concordance checks. Limits: initial generation 1 call, maximum repair calls 1. Planned analyses: primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline tested via exact McNemar two-sided procedure; sensitivity and subgroup (3×3 vendor×topology) analyses Bonferroni-corrected per preregistration. All prompts, model outputs, tool calls, hashes, and logs were preserved and are cited in the execution manifest.
sections.results: Execution summary: execution_manifest records 540 completed episodes, 0 failed episodes, and 270 model call events used (see execution/model_configuration.json and execution/execution_manifest.json). Primary outcome (registered executor paired_binary_analysis_v1): baseline accepted = 270/270 (1.00), guarded accepted = 270/270 (1.00); contingency n11=270, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0. Estimated paired difference (G−B)=0.00; exact McNemar two-sided p=1.0; 95% paired-bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (bootstrap_resamples=10000, seed=1729). Secondary outcomes: per-preregistered secondary estimands no discordant pairs observed; repair path was not invoked because verifier did not reject any shared initial candidates. Verifier validation: on the reserved validation subset and the recorded emulator checks in execution/scoring, validator verdicts aligned with emulator-ground-truth for the exercised cases (no verifier false-accept or false-reject counts were produced in the analysis artifacts). Representative examples and full scoring traces are included in execution/scoring/*.json. All analysis artifacts, contingency tables, and paired-difference figure are in analysis/ (sha256 hashes included in the artifact manifest).
sections.discussion: Interpretation: The inserted formal verifier produced no measurable improvement in this preregistered paired protocol because the generator (gpt-5-mini) produced verifier-acceptable configurations for every task under the chosen prompt/template and task-suite. This null result is informative: (1) when generations are already conservative and task abstractions are within the model’s capability, an intervening verifier with the chosen detection rules and a tight repair budget may not change end-to-end outcomes; (2) absence of detected defects does not imply safety in broader operational settings—task difficulty, adversarial inputs, model temperature, larger search spaces, or modified verifier rule-sets could change the balance; (3) a verifier can still be valuable as an auditable guard in higher-risk settings even if it does not alter outcomes in easier benchmarks. Operational implications: future evaluations should increase task hardness, introduce adversarial or out-of-distribution intents, vary model sampling/temperature, expand the repair budget, and test multiple verifier-conservatism settings.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a paired empirical evaluation of embedding a formal-network verifier as an oracle inside a bounded LLM GVR loop. Under the chosen synthetic intent→configuration suite, model (gpt-5-mini), verifier, and bounded repair budget, the guard produced no change: both baseline and guarded arms produced verifier-acceptable configurations in all N=270 tasks (paired difference 0.00, 95% CI 0.00–0.00, p=1.0). The result emphasizes that (a) a null/negative outcome is scientific evidence when the workflow was preregistered and executed reproducibly, and (b) stronger operational claims require experiments with harder tasks, adversarial conditions, broader model families, or different verifier conservatism and repair budgets. All artifacts, logs, and hashes required for reproducibility are released with the study.

Limits and scope: this study used a single hosted LLM (gpt-5-mini), a synthetic intent→configuration benchmark, a bounded repair budget (max 1 repair call per rejected candidate), and a deterministic validator/emulator for ground truth; these methodological choices and their operational consequences are declared and discussed in the manuscript. Availability: all preregistration, execution, analysis artifacts, and the full hash manifest are released with the manuscript (paths and SHA-256s appear in the supplied evidence bundle).
limitations: Synthetic task suite and limited operational realism: results may not generalize to complex, noisy, or production NetOps environments.
Single-model evaluation: only gpt-5-mini was tested; multi-model generality is untested.

Task difficulty and adversarial conditions limited: the chosen tasks were solvable by the generator under the fixed prompt/template leading to no verifier rejections; harder or adversarial tasks may yield different outcomes.
Bounded repair budget: the repair loop allowed at most one repair call per rejected candidate; larger repair budgets or multi-step repairs were not evaluated.
Verifier rule-set sensitivity: we evaluated a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); different verifier conservatism levels could change false-accept/reject trade-offs.
Emulator vs production gap: emulator-validated safety does not guarantee identical behavior on heterogeneous vendor devices or in live production networks.
